name: Cooking made us human (the fire hypothesis)
scope: Richard Wrangham's idea that controlling fire and COOKING food, not raw hunting alone, reshaped the human body and brain. T1: cooking makes food give up MORE energy than raw — heat gelatinizes starch and unfolds (denatures) protein so the gut absorbs more calories (a cooked egg or potato feeds you more than a raw one). T2: cooking does the chewing/digesting OUTSIDE the body — soft cooked food means we chew far less; a chimp eating raw must chew roughly six hours a day. T3: because cooked food is so easy to digest, the human GUT (intestines) shrank — we have a much smaller gut than an ape of our size. T4: the expensive-tissue idea (Aiello & Wheeler) — guts and brains are both metabolically 'expensive' organs, so a smaller gut freed up energy to fuel a bigger BRAIN; Homo erectus (~1.8 mya) shows exactly this combo of small jaw/teeth/gut plus a bigger brain. T5: the honest debate — WHEN fire was first controlled is contested: Wrangham argues ~1.8 mya, but firm archaeological evidence of habitual hearths is much later (~1 mya to ~400 kya), and some researchers credit meat and bone-marrow, not fire, for the change.
source: Richard Wrangham, 'Catching Fire: How Cooking Made Us Human' (2009); Scientific American 'Food for Thought: Was Cooking a Pivotal Step in Human Evolution?'; Harvard Gazette (2009); Aiello & Wheeler 'expensive tissue hypothesis' (Current Anthropology 1995); Wrangham & Carmody review, Current Anthropology 2017.
framing_note: Every rung's answer is a concrete food-energy or anatomy fact (calories unlocked, hours of chewing, gut size, brain trade-off) — keep it about FOOD mechanics, never abstract 'what is the cooking hypothesis'. Lead with a scene: the raw-vs-cooked calorie gap, the six-hours-chewing chimp. ACCURACY RAIL: present the TIMING of fire control as debated — label Wrangham's early ~1.8 mya date as his hypothesis, not settled fact. Dinner-test payoff is the expensive-tissue rung (T4): a shrinking gut paid for a growing brain.

name: The first bread, before farming (Natufian flatbread)
scope: The oldest known bread is older than farming itself, made by hunter-gatherers. T1: the oldest bread ever found is ~14,400 years old, baked by Natufian hunter-gatherers at Shubayqa in the Black Desert of Jordan — about 4,000 years BEFORE anyone farmed. T2: it was a flatbread of ground WILD cereals (wild einkorn-type wheat and barley) mixed with a surprising second ingredient — the starchy pounded tubers of a wetland plant, club-rush. T3: the grain was WILD, not planted — people gathered, ground, and baked wild wheat long before they domesticated it, so the bread came first; some argue the appetite for bread helped push people toward farming. T4: the method — grind grain on a stone quern, mix with water into a stiff dough, bake on hot stones or in ash; no oven and no leavening, so it was flat and cracker-like.
source: Arranz-Otaegui, Gonzalez Carretero et al., 'Archaeobotanical evidence reveals the origins of bread 14,400 years ago in northeastern Jordan', PNAS 2018; Biblical Archaeology Society news; Archaeology Magazine Top-10 Discoveries 2018.
framing_note: Answer is always a concrete fact about the bread — its age, its wild ingredients, its no-oven method. Scene-led: open on the record ('the oldest loaf ever found predates farming — by how long?'), invert the wonder. ACCURACY RAIL: it was WILD cereals plus club-rush tuber, NOT domesticated wheat, and it was flat/unleavened — no anachronistic yeast-risen loaf. Dinner-test payoff: the reversal that bread came BEFORE the farm (T1/T3).

name: The Agricultural Revolution and the eight founder crops
scope: Farming began in the Fertile Crescent with a tiny starter set of plants. T1: agriculture was born in the Fertile Crescent (the Middle-Eastern curve through the Levant and Mesopotamia) ~10,000-11,000 years ago, and a handful of 'founder crops' started it all. T2: the founding cereals were emmer and einkorn WHEAT and BARLEY — the wild grasses whose seed early farmers began replanting. T3: the protein came from PULSES — lentil, pea, chickpea — sown beside the grain; grain + pulse together make a near-complete protein, which is why the pairing survives everywhere (hummus-and-pita, rice-and-beans, dal-and-rice). T4: the key change that makes a plant 'domesticated' is that its seed head stopped SHATTERING — wild grain scatters its seed to reproduce, but the rare mutant that held onto its seed was useless in the wild and perfect to harvest, so farmers unknowingly selected it. T5: farming was invented INDEPENDENTLY more than once — rice in China, maize and squash in Mexico — not spread from one cradle; the Fertile Crescent was simply first.
source: Zohary, Hopf & Weiss, 'Domestication of Plants in the Old World'; Fuller et al. on Neolithic founder crops, Current Anthropology 2011; Founder crops (Wikipedia / Grokipedia, verified against those studies).
framing_note: Answer is always a specific crop or a concrete domestication fact (the founding grain, the pulse pairing, the non-shattering seed head). Scene-led: stand in the field, look at a seed head. ACCURACY RAIL: the founder crops are Old-World only (wheat/barley/lentil/pea/chickpea/flax) — NO maize, rice, or potato in the Fertile Crescent; those are separate origins, which is exactly the T5 payoff. Dinner-test payoff: the non-shattering seed head (T4) — the invisible genetic switch that made harvesting possible.

name: Taming the first food animals
scope: The first livestock were domesticated in the same Fertile Crescent, and the story is one of choosing the tameable. T1: the earliest farm animals appeared ~10,500 years ago in the Fertile Crescent, and the very first were GOATS and SHEEP — small, herd-following animals that eat grass humans can't. T2: cattle descend from the AUROCHS, a huge fierce wild ox (now extinct) — herders slowly bred a 1,800-pound wild bull's line down into the cow. T3: the PIG was domesticated from the wild BOAR, and it happened independently in two places, the Near East AND China — the same animal tamed twice. T4: why these animals and not zebras or gazelles? The tameable ones share traits — they eat cheap plants, breed readily in captivity, grow fast, and live in a calm herd hierarchy a human can slot into as 'leader' (Diamond's domestication criteria). T5: the 'secondary products' shift — at first animals were kept only for MEAT, but people later discovered a live animal gives more over time (milk, wool, and muscle for plowing) than a dead one.
source: Melinda Zeder, 'Domestication and early agriculture in the Mediterranean Basin', PNAS 2008; Jared Diamond, 'Guns, Germs, and Steel' (domestication criteria); Domestication (Wikipedia / Grokipedia, verified against Zeder).
framing_note: Answer is always a specific animal or a concrete herding/food fact. Scene-led: the wild aurochs charging, the pig tamed twice on two continents. Keep any butchery wording matter-of-fact for a kid, never gory. ACCURACY RAIL: cattle came from the AUROCHS (extinct — don't call it just 'a big cow'); goats and sheep came FIRST, cattle and pig a bit later. Dinner-test payoff: the aurochs behind every cow (T2), or the secondary-products insight that a live cow out-feeds a dead one (T5).

name: Beer and bread grew up together (Mesopotamia)
scope: In Sumer, beer and bread were the same technology and everyday food. T1: in ancient Sumer/Mesopotamia beer was daily food-drink for everyone (thick, nourishing, and safer than river water) — they even honored a goddess of beer, Ninkasi. T2: bread and beer are the SAME chemistry — grain plus yeast; Sumerians baked a special twice-baked barley loaf ('bappir') and crumbled it into water to brew, so the brewery and the bakery were cousins. T3: they drank it through long STRAWS from a shared jar, because unfiltered ancient beer had husks and gunk floating on top and the straw reached the clean liquid below (shown on a ~4,600-year-old cylinder seal from Ur). T4: the 'beer before bread?' debate — some archaeologists argue the wish to brew, not only to eat, may have been a reason people first bothered to farm grain.
source: 'The Hymn to Ninkasi', World History Encyclopedia; Ur cylinder-seal (drinking through straws, c. 2600 BCE); Peter Damerow, 'Sumerian Beer: The Origins of Brewing Technology in Ancient Mesopotamia'.
framing_note: Answer is always a concrete beer/bread/grain fact (the beer goddess, the bappir bread, the straw, the shared jar). Scene-led. ACCURACY RAIL: the Hymn to Ninkasi (~1800 BCE) is a praise-POEM that doubles as a recipe — call it a hymn, not a 'recipe book'; ancient beer was thick and unfiltered, which is WHY the straws existed. Dinner-test payoff: bread and beer are one grain-and-yeast chemistry / the straws-through-the-scum rung (T2 or T3).

name: Garum: Rome's fermented fish sauce
scope: The salty umami condiment that flavored the Roman world. T1: Romans splashed a fermented FISH sauce called garum on almost everything — their ketchup-and-soy-sauce in one, the savory backbone of Roman cooking. T2: how it's made — pack whole small fish (guts and all) in SALT and leave them in the sun for months; they break down into a clear savory liquid drawn off the top, while the leftover paste ('allec') was the cheap version for the poor. T3: WHY it tastes so good is UMAMI — fermentation frees glutamate, the same savory amino acid in parmesan and soy sauce, so garum was the ancient world's savory-flavor bomb. T4: it never died — the very same idea lives on as Southeast Asian fish sauce (Vietnamese nuoc mam, Thai nam pla), watered-down in Worcestershire sauce, and as colatura, still made in the Italian town of Cetara.
source: Garum (Wikipedia / Grokipedia, verified); National Geographic 'What Is Garum?'; The Conversation, 'why ancient Romans loved fermented fish sauces like garum' (2024); Robert Curtis on Roman fish sauce; colatura di Cetara.
framing_note: Prep-frame is fine ('you layer the fish in salt and wait') — keep the fish-guts wording matter-of-fact, never played for gross-out. Answer is always a concrete garum fact. ACCURACY RAIL: garum is SALT-fermented and controlled, not simply rotten/spoiled — the salt is what keeps it safe; it is Mediterranean, and Asia's fish sauces arose independently, not from Rome. Dinner-test payoff: garum is pure umami and the direct cousin of the fish sauce on the shelf today (T3/T4).

name: Bread and circuses: the Roman grain dole
scope: Food-driven history where the FOOD is the anchor — Rome feeding a million people. T1: the city of Rome fed hundreds of thousands of its citizens with free or cheap GRAIN, the 'grain dole' — the largest food program of the ancient world. T2: what they actually handed out was raw WHEAT — a fixed monthly ration people carried home to grind and bake themselves (free baked bread came only much later, under Aurelian). T3: where the grain came from — after Rome annexed EGYPT, the Nile valley's wheat harvest became Rome's 'breadbasket,' shipped by grain fleets to the port of Ostia. T4: 'bread and circuses' (panem et circenses) was the poet Juvenal's jab that the people would trade their freedom for free food and games — a food handout as raw political power.
source: Cura annonae (Wikipedia / Grokipedia, verified); Juvenal, Satire X ('panem et circenses'); Paul Erdkamp, 'The Grain Market in the Roman Empire'.
framing_note: The FOOD is the anchor of every rung (the wheat ration, the Egyptian breadbasket, the grain fleet) — this is food-driven history, NOT Roman politics for its own sake, and never a bare policy/date answer. Scene-led: the grain ships crossing to Ostia. ACCURACY RAIL: the dole was mostly GRAIN/wheat that people milled and baked themselves; distributed baked bread came late (3rd c. CE) — no anachronistic 'free loaves' in the Republic. Dinner-test payoff: Egypt as Rome's breadbasket (T3), or 'bread and circuses' (T4).

name: Salt's ancient power
scope: The mineral that preserved food, moved trade, and seasoned everything. T1: before refrigeration, SALT was how you kept food from rotting — it pulls the water out of meat and fish so microbes can't grow, letting ham, salt cod, and olives last for months. T2: because it preserved food, salt was precious enough to trade like money — 'salt roads' such as Rome's Via Salaria (literally 'the Salt Road') carried it inland, and towns grew up around the salt trade. T3: the famous 'Roman soldiers were paid in salt, that's why we say salary' story is only half true — the word salary does trace to Latin sal (salt), but there is NO evidence soldiers ever received sacks of salt as wages; they were paid in coin, and this is a popular tale scholars doubt, not a proven fact. T4: HOW salt preserves is osmosis — salt on the outside draws water out of the food and out of any microbe, drying them both; the same principle drives brining and pickling. T5: salt is also one of the basic tastes AND a nutrient the body must have — too little is dangerous, which is why animals seek salt licks and why salt could command such trade.
source: Mark Kurlansky, 'Salt: A World History'; Kiwi Hellenist, 'Salt and salary: were Roman soldiers paid in salt?'; Pliny the Elder, Natural History Bk 31; Via Salaria.
framing_note: Answer is always a concrete salt-and-food fact (preservation, the salt road, osmosis). Scene-led. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the salary / 'paid in salt' etymology is CONTESTED — frame it explicitly as a popular claim scholars reject (no ancient source says it; soldiers were paid in money); the answer TEACHES the myth-vs-fact distinction and must NOT assert soldiers were paid in salt. Dinner-test payoff: the salt/salary myth-busting rung (T3), or the osmosis mechanism (T4).

name: The cooking pot: how boiling changed the menu
scope: Pottery unlocked a whole new way to cook. T1: the oldest known POTTERY — ~20,000 years old, from Xianrendong cave in China — was made by hunter-gatherers thousands of years before farming, and the shards carry scorch marks: the pots were used to COOK. T2: pottery unlocked BOILING — before a waterproof pot you couldn't easily boil, so now people could make soup, porridge, and stew, and cook things you can't roast (shellfish, tough grains, bones simmered for grease and marrow). T3: boiling makes food SOFT, which fed those without strong teeth — babies could be weaned earlier onto porridge and elders could eat again, so more people survived (a cooking technique with a population effect). T4: a pot also DETOXIFIES — long boiling breaks down bitter or poisonous compounds in some wild foods (acorns, certain tubers), turning what was inedible into a meal.
source: Wu et al., 'Early Pottery at 20,000 Years Ago in Xianrendong Cave, China', Science 2012; Science News coverage; Wrangham on boiling and plant detoxification.
framing_note: Answer is always a concrete pottery/boiling fact. Scene-led: the scorched ice-age pot, the first bubbling porridge. ACCURACY RAIL: the oldest pottery is hunter-gatherer and PRE-farming — pottery did not require agriculture, and it was used to cook. Dinner-test payoff: boiling-softens-food-and-feeds-the-toothless (T3), or the detox-by-boiling rung (T4).

name: Cheese and the first dairying
scope: Turning perishable milk into a food that lasts. T1: cheese is a way to make milk LAST — turning a food that spoils in a day into a storable solid; people were already doing it ~7,500 years ago (Neolithic pottery cheese-strainers, pierced with holes to drain the whey, found in Poland). T2: the trick that turns milk to cheese is RENNET — an enzyme from a young animal's stomach that curdles milk into solid curds and liquid whey; the classic origin story has it discovered by accident, when milk carried in a stomach-bag canteen set into curds. T3: cheese also solved a body problem — many early adults couldn't digest milk sugar (lactose) well, but fermenting milk into cheese or yogurt breaks the lactose down, so people could eat dairy before their genes caught up. T4: the oldest actual lump of cheese ever found (~3,200 years old) came from an Egyptian tomb — proof cheese was a prized food worth burying with the dead.
source: Salque et al., 'Earliest evidence for cheese making in the sixth millennium BC in northern Europe', Nature 2012; Greco et al. on the Ptahmes-tomb cheese (Egypt, ~3,200 yrs); 'the milk revolution' (Nature).
framing_note: Answer is always a concrete cheese/milk fact (the whey-draining strainer, rennet from a stomach, cheese beating lactose). Scene-led. ACCURACY RAIL: rennet comes from a young animal's STOMACH (calf/kid), and early cheese predates widespread lactose tolerance — that IS the point, don't imply ancient adults drank milk freely. Dinner-test payoff: rennet and the stomach-bag origin (T2), or cheese-lets-you-eat-dairy-early (T3).

name: Maize: from a wild grass to corn
scope: The New World's founding crop, built by ancient farmers. T1: corn (maize) does not exist in the wild — it was BUILT from a wild Mexican grass called TEOSINTE, starting ~9,000 years ago in the Balsas River valley of Mexico. T2: teosinte looks nothing like corn — a skinny stalk bearing maybe a dozen hard, stony kernels each locked in a rock-hard shell, barely food; farmers selected rare mutant plants over centuries into the big, soft, many-kerneled cob we know. T3: all corn on Earth descends from a SINGLE domestication — one grass, one region — yet it became the staple of two continents, the most dramatic human-made makeover of any crop. T4: the Three Sisters — Native American farmers grew maize, BEANS, and SQUASH together: corn is a living pole for the beans to climb, beans put nitrogen back in the soil, squash leaves shade out weeds, and corn-plus-beans together make a complete protein. T5: nixtamalization — soaking maize in wood-ash or lime water (to make masa for tortillas) isn't just softening; it unlocks the vitamin niacin the body can't get from raw corn, which is why peoples who adopted corn WITHOUT this trick suffered the deficiency disease pellagra.
source: Piperno et al. on Balsas maize origins, PNAS; Matsuoka et al. on single-origin domestication; Smithsonian 'Rethinking the Corny History of Maize'; nixtamalization / pellagra literature.
framing_note: Answer is always a concrete maize fact (teosinte, the single origin, the Three Sisters, the ash-water). Scene-led: the stony little teosinte cob beside a modern ear. ACCURACY RAIL: maize is MESOAMERICAN (from Mexican teosinte) — NOT an Old-World crop; it reached Europe, Africa, and Asia only after 1492, so no corn anywhere in the ancient Old World. Dinner-test payoff: nixtamalization unlocking a vitamin (T5), or teosinte as corn's unrecognizable ancestor (T1).

name: Wine's deep roots in the Caucasus
scope: The oldest wine, and why wine almost makes itself. T1: the oldest known wine — ~8,000 years old (around 6000 BC) — comes from the country of Georgia in the Caucasus, where chemists found grape-wine residue inside giant clay jars; wine's cradle is the Caucasus, not France or Italy. T2: they fermented and aged it in huge egg-shaped clay jars called QVEVRI, buried up to the neck in the ground to hold a steady cool temperature — a method Georgians still use today. T3: why wine 'makes itself' — wild YEAST lives on the skin of the grape, so a crushed pile of grapes begins to ferment on its own with nothing added; the first wine was almost certainly an accident of stored grapes. T4: from the Caucasus the grapevine spread as a prestige drink across the ancient Mediterranean, carried by Phoenician and Greek traders in clay amphorae, becoming central to the Greek symposium and later to religious ritual.
source: McGovern et al., 'Early Neolithic wine of Georgia in the South Caucasus', PNAS 2017; Guinness World Records / Haaretz coverage; qvevri (UNESCO intangible heritage).
framing_note: Answer is always a concrete wine/grape fact (the Georgian cradle, the buried qvevri, the wild yeast on the skin). Scene-led, invert the wonder ('the oldest wine on Earth was buried in jars — where?'). ACCURACY RAIL: the oldest wine evidence is Georgian/Caucasian (~6000 BC), older than Iran's Hajji Firuz — do NOT credit France or Italy with the origin. AVOID naming tartaric acid as the tested answer (lab jargon); it may be context only. Dinner-test payoff: wild yeast on the grape skin means 'wine makes itself' (T3).

name: Honey: the first sweetener
scope: Humanity's original concentrated sweet. T1: before sugar existed, HONEY was the only concentrated sweetener humans had — and the oldest painting of people getting food shows a figure climbing to raid a wild bees' nest (Cuevas de la Arana, Spain, ~8,000 years old). T2: honey almost never spoils — its super-high sugar and very low water pull moisture out of any microbe (bees also add a touch of acid and peroxide), which is why sealed honey found in Egyptian tombs was reportedly still edible thousands of years later. T3: Egyptians went beyond raiding wild nests — they kept bees in stacked clay-tube HIVES and even floated hives down the Nile to follow the blooming season; honey served as sweetener, medicine, and temple offering.
source: Cuevas de la Arana rock art (Wikipedia / ResearchGate figure); Eva Crane, 'The World History of Beekeeping and Honey Hunting'; ancient Egyptian beekeeping (Nyuserre sun-temple relief, c. 2450 BCE).
framing_note: Answer is always a concrete honey/bee fact (the cave honey-hunter, the never-spoiling jar, the Nile bee-boats). Scene-led: open on the 8,000-year-old climber reaching into the wild hive. ACCURACY RAIL: pre-sugar, honey was THE sweetener — cane sugar reached the West far later, so no anachronistic 'sugar' in antiquity; the Arana scene is the oldest known depiction of honey-gathering. Dinner-test payoff: why honey never spoils (T2).
